column4: “Seek help through patience and prayer” gives the section’s نَسْتَعِينُ concrete supports for a weakened traveller.
Again commands believers to seek help through patience and prayer, adding that God is with the patient when endurance is needed.
Facing Goliath, the believers ask for patience to be poured on them, firm feet, and help: a prayer for standing rather than collapsing.
The source’s q-w-m dictionary sense of a sustaining pillar meets al-Qayyūm, the ever-sustaining ground of the traveller’s reliance.
The unbreakable “firm handhold” supplies a visible support under the weak person’s grip.
The closing prayer asks that no soul bear beyond its capacity, then calls God its protector and asks for help.
After receiving guidance, believers ask that their hearts not deviate; the source’s swaying walker becomes inward instability held by mercy.
Holding all together to God’s rope turns the two-sided support of the source’s walker into communal dependence that prevents division.
Two groups are about to lose courage, but God is their protector; it stages a faltering body or community upheld before it gives way.
The prophets’ followers ask for forgiveness, firm feet, and divine help, directly joining inner repair to upright footing.
“If God helps you” no one can overcome you, and if He leaves you no one can help: the verse fixes the true source of support.
The source’s q-w-m family calls qiyām a support; this ayah calls wealth qiyāman for people, a material means by which life stands.
God wants to lighten the burden because the human being was created weak, naming the bodily need that makes help necessary.
The oppressed weak men, women, and children ask God for a guardian and a helper, a direct social form of the assisted traveller.
Those who hold fast to God receive mercy and are guided to a straight path; grasping support and receiving direction occur together.
The source’s q-w-m uprightness becomes ethical in qawwāmīn for justice, standing firmly even when testimony cuts against oneself.
“Cooperate in righteousness and reverence” makes believers one another’s practical عون, as the source says help is whatever one relies on.
Qawwāmīn for God must not let hatred bend them from justice, extending the source’s upright stance to a moral refusal to swerve.
The Kaʿbah and sacred ordinances are qiyāman for people; the source’s q-w-m support becomes an institution that steadies a community.
A bewildered person is driven about on earth while companions call him to guidance; this is the assisted, unsteady traveller reversed by refusing God’s هدًى.
Stars guide travellers through the darknesses of land and sea, giving ihdinā’s guidance a literal wayfinding scene.
One made alive receives a light and walks among people, unlike one trapped in darkness; the image makes guided walking a supported bodily passage.
God’s single straight path is to be followed, while other paths split a person away from it; the source’s upright route has a concrete boundary.
Satan waits on the straight path to obstruct it, the hostile counterpart to the supports sought by the traveller.
Moses tells his people, “Seek help from God and be patient,” directly pairing istiʿānah with the endurance that keeps them standing.
The believers cry to their Lord for rescue and He answers with angels; requested help is answered by companions sent to reinforce them.
God binds their hearts and makes their feet firm; inner fastening and physical footing realize the source’s body being held upright.
God tells the angels to strengthen the believers, another explicit scene of divine helpers bracing those who would otherwise falter.
A few oppressed people afraid of being seized are sheltered, aided, and provided for; help changes exposed weakness into secure standing.
Calling God the excellent protector and excellent helper states the dependable support behind requests for assistance.
In the cave God sends tranquillity and supports the Prophet with unseen forces, showing aid arriving when a traveller is isolated.
Those who come seeking a mount are turned away because none is available; their grief gives the source’s stranded rider a Qur’anic scene.
A building founded on a crumbling cliff falls with its maker, the opposite of the source’s restored wall and sound support.
After Moses and Aaron pray, they are told to remain steadfast; a plea for God’s action becomes an instruction to stand straight.
“Be steadfast as commanded” gives mustaqīm its standing force, asking the messenger and companions to maintain an upright course.
Shuʿayb says his success is only through God and that he relies on Him, naming reliance as the condition of acting rightly.
Jacob’s “beautiful patience” and “God is the One whose help is sought” directly join the source’s istiʿānah to endurance under shock.
The messengers ask why they should not rely on God when He has guided them in their ways: guidance supplies the ground for dependence.
The source’s q-w-m tree image is explicit here: a good word is a tree with roots firmly fixed and branches raised.
The evil word is an uprooted tree with no stability, reversing the source’s standing tree rooted in support.
God makes believers firm by the firm word in this life and the next, turning rootedness into sustained human uprightness.
Pack animals carry human burdens to lands people could reach only with hardship, directly answering the source’s exhausted rider and mount.
The direction of the way belongs to God and some paths are crooked; this supplies a divine measure for the straight route requested in 1:6.
Landmarks and stars guide people, a second literal navigation scene for the traveller who cannot find the way alone.
God brings down the roof of plotters’ building from its foundations, a collapse that clarifies what the raised wall of 18:77 resists.
The Qur’an guides to what is aqwam, joining the source’s h-d-y request to q-w-m’s most upright and sound condition.
The command not to walk exultantly on earth bounds the source’s calm, well-guided gait by rejecting proud strutting.
God made the Prophet firm; without that support he would have inclined a little. It is the source’s swaying body steadied from collapse.
The prayer for a truthful entrance and exit asks God for “supporting authority,” making divine backing accompany every movement through a passage.
The cave youths ask for mercy and for right guidance in their affair, a compact prayer for the help and direction of a vulnerable group.
God binds the youths’ hearts when they stand up; fastening the inner support and standing bodily meet in one scene.
After their withdrawal, the youths are promised mercy and ease in their affair; it completes the aid requested in 18:10.
Whom God guides is guided, and one He leaves astray has no guiding protector; the verse makes guidance inseparable from sustaining patronage.
Moses and his companion acknowledge fatigue from their journey, an actual travel-weariness before the encounter with the divinely taught servant.
The servant is given mercy and knowledge by God; those gifts make him a divinely supplied guide in the journey that reaches the failing wall.
Moses asks whether he may follow the servant to learn right guidance, staging a traveller who needs another’s taught direction.
The wall about to collapse is erected. The source’s q-w-m sense of setting upright turns failed cohesion into standing protection.
A threatened people ask Dhū al-Qarnayn to make a barrier for them, giving vulnerability a communal, protective form.
“Help me with strength” produces a rampart; requested assistance becomes the force that makes a standing barrier possible.
Worshipping the one Lord is named the straight path, explicitly tying the section’s naʿbudu to the path that follows it.
Abraham tells his father, “Follow me; I will guide you to a straight path,” making guidance an offered companionship in motion.
Moses asks for an expanded breast, beginning his mission with an inward capacity widened for a weight he cannot carry alone.
“Make my task easy” gives the source’s weak traveller a direct prophetic request for an eased passage.
Moses asks for a minister from his family, making assistance take the form of a companion at his side.
“Strengthen my back through him” is the clearest bodily counterpart to the source’s traveller leaning on supports.
Making Aaron share the task explains why the helper is sought: burden-bearing becomes a joint work rather than solitary strain.
God tells Moses and Aaron not to fear because He is with them, giving their paired mission an unseen supporting presence.
When Moses feels fear, God tells him not to fear and assures him of the upper hand, a direct act of stabilizing a shaken servant.
Whoever follows God’s guidance will neither go astray nor suffer; supported following is set against the traveller’s feared loss of way.
“Our Lord is the Merciful, the One whose help is sought” reunites the source’s Rabb, Raḥmān, and istiʿānah in one prophetic appeal.
One worships God on an edge and turns on his face when tried, a precarious reversal of worship that steadies and directs.
Pilgrims come on foot and on every lean camel from deep passes, bringing fatigued bodies and mounts directly into the journey image.
God places no hardship in the religion and is the excellent protector and helper, framing worship as held within divine support.
The Prophet calls people to a straight path; the verse preserves the guiding voice that the source’s dependent traveller needs.
The Lord is sufficient as both guide and helper, joining h-d-y and aid in the exact roles separated by the source’s image.
The servants of the Merciful walk gently upon earth, the Qur’anic counterpart to the source’s calm, beautiful gait.
The same servants spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord; after 25:63, their gentle walk opens into bodily worship.
Trapped before the sea, Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him; divine presence supplies direction at the moment of no way forward.
God guides through the darknesses of land and sea and sends the winds of mercy, a literal rescue-guide for disoriented travellers.
Setting out toward Midian, Moses asks that his Lord guide him to the right way, a traveller’s explicit need for direction.
After reaching the water, Moses confesses need for whatever good God sends; the tired traveller’s dependence becomes a prayer.
The woman comes walking with modest reserve to answer Moses’s need in 28:24; her gait and her help complete a quiet support scene.
Even love cannot make a person guided; God alone guides whom He wills, marking the limit of any human companion’s help.
Those who strive for God are guided in His paths; effort is not solitary but answered with routes opened by divine guidance.
The source’s m-l-k image of failed cohesion is reversed in the spider’s house: false protectors provide the weakest house.
A human caller cannot guide the blind away from error, a boundary on the outward guide when the traveller cannot receive direction.
Human life moves from weakness to strength and back to weakness; the source’s frail body is a created condition, not an incidental failure.
Do not walk boastfully on earth: the source’s composed gait is clarified by its proud, self-sufficient opposite.
“Be moderate in your walk” directly gives form to the source’s unhurried, well-guided movement.
Submitting to God while doing good is grasping the firmest handhold, renewing the bodily image of a support that will not fail.
Leaders are made to guide by God’s command after patience and certainty; guidance here arises through endured weakness rather than self-sufficiency.
People are needy of God while God is free of need; the source’s helpless traveller becomes the human condition before its only sufficient support.
God holds the heavens and earth lest they slip away, a cosmic enactment of the source’s sustaining, upright support.
“Worship Me; this is a straight path” explicitly makes worship the road that the source’s naʿbudu asks to be helped along.
“Is God not sufficient for His servant?” names the sufficiency beneath the servant’s request for aid.
The believing man says, “Follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct,” another voiced offer of guidance to a follower.
The command to be steadfast toward God turns the source’s mustaqīm from a flat road into an upright, directed human stance.
Thamūd prefer blindness to guidance after being shown it, reversing the weak traveller who accepts help to walk rightly.
Those who say “Our Lord is God” and then stand firm receive descending angels and the assurance not to fear or grieve.
God makes paths in the earth so people may be guided, preparing traversable ground for the traveller’s request.
God makes ships and cattle for riding, supplying the mount that the source’s exhausted traveller lacks.
When riders settle on their mounts, they remember the One who subjected them, admitting this carrying power is received rather than self-made.
Holding fast to revelation and being on a straight path joins a secure grip to directed movement.
Worshipping the one Lord is called the straight path, again making service to God the route rather than a separate act.
Those who say “Our Lord is God” then stand firm have no fear or grief, a promised outcome for sustained uprightness.
If believers support God’s cause, He supports them and makes their feet firm; help is rendered as stable footing.
The believing community is likened to a plant that grows strong and stands upon its stalk, extending the rooted, upright body into a community.
Book and balance are sent so people may stand for justice; revelation becomes the support by which a people stand upright.
Faith brings mercy and a light in which to walk, making divine support into illumination for actual forward movement.
The source’s dictionary example is Qur’anic here: date palms are left standing on their roots, a literal image of stable uprightness.
Those who stand in ranks are like a solidly joined structure; the source’s wall-cohesion image becomes mutual human firmness.
Whoever relies on God finds Him sufficient; this names the support on which the source’s unable traveller can actually lean.
God, Gabriel, righteous believers, and angels are named as backers, turning the source’s two supporting sides into layered help.
Earth is made tractable so people may walk its paths and receive provision, showing terrain itself prepared for a dependent walker.
The face-down walker is contrasted with one walking upright on a straight path, the section’s two bodily gaits stated outright.
God spreads earth as a carpet; 71:20 completes its use as ground on which people traverse broad paths.
The broad paths of 71:20 depend on the spread earth of 71:19, making prepared ground part of guided passage.
Had they remained steadfast on the way, God would have given abundant water; upright persistence on a path receives sustaining provision.
God removes the burden from the Prophet; 94:3 identifies it as one that weighed down his back, the body’s need for relief.
The burden that weighed on the back gives bodily force to the relief announced in 94:2.
“With hardship comes ease” makes the source’s passage from exhaustion to supported movement a promised pairing.
The repeated ease of 94:6 reinforces the relief paired with hardship in 94:5, rather than leaving the burden as the final state.
When divine guidance comes, whoever follows it will neither go astray nor grieve; the dependent traveller’s safety is made conditional on following guidance.
Believers are shaken by adversity until they ask when God’s help will come; the answer that it is near gives requested aid a crisis scene.
Standing devoutly before God in prayer makes the source’s q-w-m bodily uprightness part of worship itself.
An indirect but concrete reversal of the stalled mount: a passerby is shown his dead donkey restored, so a stopped journey becomes a sign of renewed life.
Jesus names worship of the one Lord as the straight path, repeating the source section’s movement from naʿbudu to the requested road.
Jesus asks who will be his helpers toward God, and the disciples answer that they are God’s helpers; aid becomes companions who stand with a messenger.
Holding fast to God is followed by being guided to a straight path, joining a secure grip to directed movement.
God promises to reinforce the vulnerable believers with sent-down angels, another answer in which help takes the form of supporting companions.
The angelic reinforcement is made good news so hearts may be reassured; its own contribution is the inner steadiness that aid is meant to give.
Threatened believers answer that God is sufficient and the best disposer of affairs, an enacted refusal to seek a less reliable support.
The oppressed weak people cannot devise a plan or find a way, directly naming those who need both help and guidance.
Travel permits a shortened prayer under threat, showing worship itself eased for a vulnerable traveller rather than imposed as an added weight.
By the Book, God leads seekers of His approval along paths of peace, out of darkness and onto a straight path.
Guidance opens the breast, while misguidance constricts it; the source’s supported body has an inner counterpart in expanded or compressed capacity.
The speaker is guided to a straight path described as an upright religion, tightly joining h-d-y to the source’s q-w-m uprightness.
Following the cry for aid in 8:9, this ayah says the angelic response reassures hearts while victory remains from God; it distinguishes the help’s means from its source.
Those who give shelter and help to emigrants become allies of those displaced believers, a social realization of the traveller being held up by others.
The later restatement that migrants and those who shelter and help them are true believers preserves mutual support as a defining communal act.
In the hour of hardship some hearts nearly swerved, yet God turns mercifully toward the Prophet, emigrants, and helpers, preventing inner collapse.
God, who guides to truth, is contrasted with one unable to guide unless first guided; it tests which leader a dependent traveller should follow.
After 11:112’s command to stand firm, this ayah forbids inclining toward wrongdoers and warns that no protector or help remains there.
Jacob again answers loss with “beautiful patience,” extending 12:18’s supported endurance into a second, renewed deprivation.
The messengers admit their human likeness and say believers should rely on God, grounding prophetic action in received favor rather than personal sufficiency.
Satan admits that he merely called and cannot rescue those who followed him; it is a false guide and false helper exposed at the end.
Mountains keep earth from swaying with people, while rivers and paths are made so they may be guided; stable footing and wayfinding are paired.
The Spirit brings revelation to strengthen believers, explicitly naming it both guidance and good news; the guide fortifies the one who receives it.
After forgetting, the Prophet asks that his Lord guide him to what is nearer to right conduct, a precise request for corrected direction.
The ruined garden owner has no group to help him against God and cannot defend himself, exposing support that disappears when it is most needed.
Zachariah says his bones have weakened and turns to God in prayer, a concrete bodily weakness that seeks help without self-reliance.
Firm mountains prevent the earth from swaying with people, and wide paths are set in it so they may be guided: support against wobbling becomes guidance.
The House is purified for those circling, standing, bowing, and prostrating; beside 22:27’s arriving pilgrims, it supplies the upright worship at journey’s end.
The Qur’an is sent in stages to strengthen the Prophet’s heart; the source’s dictionary image of the heart as the body’s support gains a direct Qur’anic counterpart.
God binds Moses’s mother’s heart when grief nearly makes her reveal him, a vivid scene of an inner support preventing a person from giving way.
The Prophet is told to rely on God, who is sufficient as disposer of affairs; reliance is stated as an adequate support for action.
The command to lead the guilty to the path of Hell reverses the life-giving horizon of guidance and warns that being led is not itself salvific.
The Prophet is said to guide to a straight path, identifying the prophetic voice through which a seeker of ihdinā receives direction.
Those who turn back on their heels after guidance has become clear show the reverse movement of the source’s assisted traveller continuing forward.
God sends tranquillity into believers’ hearts so their faith may increase, giving communal firmness an inward support.
The settled believers welcome and prefer the emigrants despite their own need, showing support that lets displaced people continue rather than remain stranded.
“Be helpers of God” is illustrated by Jesus’s disciples answering his call for helpers, a second explicit model of companions lending strength.
The command for “beautiful patience” repeats Jacob’s phrase in 12:18, making patient composure a continuing discipline under pressure.
No one can protect the speaker from God and no refuge exists apart from Him, drawing the boundary around every lesser support.
God knows that the Prophet and believers cannot sustain the full measure of night standing, so He relieves them and commands what is easy of recitation.
God promises to ease the messenger toward ease, a concise divine answer to the source’s passage from strain to supported movement.
God finds the Prophet wandering and guides him, making a person once without a way the recipient of direct divine direction.
Humanity is created in the best taqwīm; this q-w-m form gives the source’s upright body a created, bodily ground.
Being returned to the lowest of the low reverses the upright taqwīm of 95:4, marking how bodily or moral standing can be lost.
